title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 25-32
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 25-32 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: An approval and a kill switch differ in the scope of what they gate. How?
options: An approval gates one action, while a kill switch stops the whole run
An approval stops the whole run, while a kill switch gates exactly one action
Both gate one action, so neither can halt a runaway loop
Both stop the whole run, so neither gates one action
questions.explanation: The controls are ranked by scope: an approval gates the smallest unit, one action, while a kill switch is the widest control and stops the whole run.

questions.question: Why must an approval gate live in the runtime rather than in the system prompt?
options: Model providers reject any prompt that names more than one tool
A prompt is guidance a model may ignore; a runtime gate always fires
System prompts cannot persist across the steps of a tool-calling loop
A runtime cannot read a tool definition that the model was given
questions.explanation: A control must be a mechanism the runtime enforces, not a preference the model may or may not follow; a prompt only asks, while a deterministic gate holds.

questions.question: What is the defining test of a real kill switch?
options: It asks the model to stop once it detects that it is looping
It pauses a single action until a person approves or rejects it
It can stop every running instance without the agent's cooperation
It records the runaway so a person can stop it after reviewing the record
questions.explanation: A kill switch is deterministic and external: it must be able to end the run without the agent's consent, which is why it is a cap the system enforces rather than a tool the agent chooses to call.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between the requests-per-minute and tokens-per-minute limits?
options: Requests per minute counts input and output, so large prompts trip it before token count
Both limits count only output tokens, so prompt size never affects either one
Tokens per minute counts input and output, so large prompts trip it before request count
Both limits count only input tokens, so answer length is never limited at all
questions.explanation: Tokens per minute counts combined input and output tokens, so a workload with large prompts exhausts the token ceiling long before its request count matters.

questions.question: How does continuous batching improve throughput over naive batching?
options: It admits new requests as slots free, instead of holding a fixed batch together
It runs every request alone in isolation so none can block any of the others
It sorts all incoming requests by their length before running them as a single fixed batch
It caches the model weights once so that only the first request pays a premium
questions.explanation: Continuous batching lets a finished sequence leave at each decoding step and a waiting request take its slot, so the hardware stops idling while it waits for the slowest member of a batch.

questions.question: Why is a rate limit alone not enough to protect the budget?
options: It caps total spend, so it never limits how quickly a tenant can send requests
It applies only to input tokens, leaving every output token entirely uncapped and unmeasured
It resets every minute, so it cannot be measured against any monthly budget
It caps speed, so a run within every limit can still spend without bound over a month
questions.explanation: A rate limit controls speed while a budget controls total spend, so a runaway that stays within every per-minute limit can still bill for a large sum until a dollar or token cap stops it.

questions.question: In what order should the cost levers be applied, and why?
options: Cap, then cache, then route, since a budget ceiling stops overspending right away
Cache, then route across tiers, then cap and watch, since the first two set the amount spent
Watch first, then cap, then route, since a spend dashboard shows exactly where the money went
Route first, then watch, then cache, since per-token pricing gaps are the single biggest lever
questions.explanation: Caching and routing reduce how much is spent before any cap matters; a dashboard only reports where the money went, so reaching for it first leaves the bill unchanged.

questions.question: Why can a cheaper model end up costing more?
options: A lower price per token always lowers the total bill no matter what the task actually involves
Cheaper models can never be called as often as a frontier model can be
Cheaper models bill in a separate currency that is significantly harder to track
A lower price per token can raise cost per task when its mistakes force retries or review
questions.explanation: The metric that matters is cost per completed task, not cost per token, because a cheap model that makes mistakes can cost more downstream than the frontier model would have.

questions.question: What is the risk of a semantic cache with a loose similarity threshold?
options: It can return an answer that only resembles the question, which is a correctness bug
It stores every cached answer twice, roughly doubling the storage cost of the cache itself
It refuses almost every cache hit, calling the model for each request again
It slows the first call in each window while the cached prefix is written
questions.explanation: A semantic cache decides a hit by embedding similarity, so a loose threshold starts serving answers that merely resemble the question, which makes the threshold a correctness decision and not only a cost one.

questions.question: Why is proving an agent's identity not enough to decide what it may do?
options: They are the same check, so a single successful login grants full access to everything
Identity only matters for a person, so an agent's identity carries no permissions of its own
Identity is established once per session, so permissions never need to be checked again later
They are separate checks, so authentication alone does not grant every action
questions.explanation: Authentication proves who is acting and authorization decides what that actor may do; treating them as one check is broken access control, because a proven identity is not automatically permitted for everything.

questions.question: Why is a credential in the model's context window a special problem for an agent?
options: The context window is far too small to hold both the credential and the user request
The model can repeat it or be steered into revealing it, so it is as good as leaked
The model charges extra tokens for any credential it reads inside its context
A credential left in context slows down every later call in the same session
questions.explanation: Everything an agent reads lands in its context window, so a credential there is not configuration anymore but data the model can be steered into repeating, which is why secrets are injected at the boundary instead.

questions.question: When should an agent's permissions be checked?
options: Once at the start of the session, since the agent's identity does not change during the run
Only when a tool writes state, since read-only calls can never be harmful
On every request, since one unchecked call in a long session is enough to exploit
Once per day, at the moment when the operator rotates the agent's credentials
questions.explanation: An agent session can run dozens of tool calls and each one needs its own authorization check, because a single unchecked call is the one an attacker finds.

questions.question: What does data residency actually require of an agent's data path?
options: That every system touching the data has a lawful basis for where its bytes land
That all of the data be stored inside one country regardless of the governing law
That the front-end region selector be set correctly before each request
That data be encrypted at rest so its location no longer matters legally
questions.explanation: The front-end region is only one touchpoint; the model provider, vector store, trace store, and log store are each a jurisdiction, and every one of them needs a lawful basis for where it processes data.

questions.question: What separates an audit log from an ordinary observability log?
options: It stores the full prompts and all raw personal data, while a trace store does not
It is written only after the whole run finishes, while the observability log is live
It must be automatic, complete, and append-only so the past cannot be rewritten
It is held in memory, while the observability log is written out to disk
questions.explanation: An observability log is a working tool for debugging, while an audit log is evidence: it must be recorded automatically, cover every action, and survive as written so the record proves something.

questions.question: How is the tension between audit retention and data-protection deletion resolved?
options: Keep every prompt and every raw record forever so no audit obligation can ever be missed
Retain the compliance metadata, and expire the personal payload on a short schedule
Delete the entire audit trail quickly so that no personal data is retained at all
Keep the raw personal data and delete the metadata, since metadata is easily replaced
questions.explanation: The record that proves compliance is the metadata, such as who acted when and with which tools, while the raw personal data it processed can be expired on a short automated schedule.

questions.question: What core problem does the MCP protocol exist to solve?
options: Bespoke integrations grow as apps times tools; one protocol replaces them
Models cannot call any function at all without a vendor-specific software kit
Agents respond far too slowly to remain useful once they run in production
Tool schemas are so large that they cannot fit inside a model's context window
questions.explanation: Without a shared standard, each application needs a hand-written connector for every tool, so the maintenance grows as the product of the two; one protocol collapses that to a single connector on each side.

questions.question: In the MCP architecture, what is the client?
options: A separate machine that runs both the model and the whole orchestration
A component inside the host, created once per server connection
The remote program that exposes tools, prompts, and data
The end user's browser session that opens the connection
questions.explanation: The client is not a separate machine: it lives inside the host and the host creates one client object for each server it connects to, handling that single connection's protocol messages.

questions.question: For a local server that communicates over stdio, why must it never write to standard output?
options: Standard output is reserved for the model's own streamed tokens and its replies
Standard output is much slower than standard error and would slow the server down
Standard output cannot safely carry structured JSON and would break the entire tool schema
Standard output carries the protocol messages, so stray output corrupts the stream
questions.explanation: A stdio server sends its JSON-RPC messages over standard output, so a stray print statement corrupts that stream and breaks the server, which is why diagnostics go to standard error.

questions.question: Who decides when each MCP server primitive is used?
options: The model calls resources, the user attaches tools, and the application selects prompts
The application calls every primitive, and the model only supplies arguments
The model calls tools, the application attaches resources, and the user selects prompts
The user selects every primitive, and the model only supplies arguments
questions.explanation: The three primitives are controlled by different parties: the model decides to call tools, the application decides which resources to place in context, and the user selects prompts.

questions.question: Why did the protocol move away from sampling?
options: Sampling was far too slow to run inside a request-response exchange with the client
Sampling required a human in the loop, which the specification decided to forbid entirely
Sampling only worked over stdio and never over a remote HTTP transport
Inference moved out of the protocol, so a server should call a provider API directly
questions.explanation: Sampling once let a server borrow the client's model without holding its own keys, but the protocol moved inference out of scope in favor of a server calling an LLM provider API directly.

questions.question: Why does a remote MCP server bind a token to itself with the resource parameter?
options: So a token for one server cannot be replayed against a different server
So the server can pass the token downstream to other APIs on the user's behalf
So the authorization server can avoid running a PKCE authorization code flow
So the client can skip sending an Authorization header on later requests
questions.explanation: The resource parameter binds a token to one specific server, so a token minted for one audience cannot be replayed against another; a server must also never forward a client's token downstream.

questions.question: Why should an enterprise agent project start from a problem bounded in one sentence?
options: A one-sentence scope lets the agent run without any tools or permissions at all
A narrow scope removes the need for any test set or a defined success condition
Every downstream choice, tools, permissions, and evals, follows from that boundary
A vague scope is acceptable as long as the underlying model is large and capable enough
questions.explanation: A boundary the agent can state in one sentence determines its tools, its permissions, and its evaluation set, which is why a vague ambition lets scope grow to fill the empty repository.

questions.question: How should an enterprise agent project handle its secrets and environment?
options: Commit the keys directly in the repository so every teammate and tool can find them
Keep secrets in a git-ignored environment file and ship a documented example
Hard-code the keys in the agent source so the model can reference them
Store the keys in the model's system prompt so it can authenticate its tools
questions.explanation: Secrets belong in the environment and out of version control, so the repository keeps a documented example file with no real keys and the environment file is git-ignored.

questions.question: Why start with the framework's in-memory state and move to a durable store only later?
options: It is simple for local runs, but it vanishes on restart and is not shared
It is the only option available until the agent has been deployed to production
A durable store cannot be adopted until the agent has well over a hundred tools
It persists across restarts, so a durable store is never actually needed
questions.explanation: In-memory state is fine for local graphs and tests, but it disappears on restart and is not shared across workers, so a durable store is needed before you rely on resuming a run.
